definitions.text: The total number of protons and neutrons present in an atom almost accounts for the total mass of that atom and hence it is called its nucleon number or mass number.
Atoms of the same element having different number of neutrons in their nuclei are called isotopes.
The relative atomic mass of an element is thus defined as the mass of an atom of that element relative to the mass of light isotope of carbon taken as 12.
It is defined as one-twelfth the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
Since an atom, as a whole, is electrically neutral, the number of electrons present in an atom will be the same as the number of protons.

formulas.use: Find neutrons in an atom: N, A and Z are particle counts (dimensionless; no SI units).
Find a shell’s maximum electron capacity: n is the shell number and the capacity is a particle count (both dimensionless; no SI units).
Find average relative atomic mass from isotope masses and percentage abundances: m values and p values are dimensionless, so the result is dimensionless (no SI units).

A short, central concept linking different atoms to different element properties.
A standard calculation using the chapter’s neutron-number formula.
A direct explanation of shell distance and energy, suitable for a constructed response.
Tests the conditions used in the key discharge-tube experiment.

fullMarks: For an atom written as ᴬ_ZX, identify A as the mass number and Z as the atomic number before finding its particles.
For a neutron calculation, write N = A − Z, substitute the values, and state the final number of neutrons.
For a neutral atom, state that the number of electrons equals the number of protons; do not assume this for an ion.
When explaining shell energy, say that the second shell is farther from the nucleus than the first and has greater energy.
For questions about electron models, describe the definite shells in Bohr’s model first, then contrast them with the modern probability-cloud idea.
For a relative atomic mass calculation, show the weighted-abundance formula, substitute every isotope mass and abundance, divide by 100, and give the result clearly. Relative atomic mass has no unit.
When explaining why the nucleus contains almost all the atom’s mass, name both protons and neutrons as the heavy particles and mention the strong nuclear force holds them together.
mistakes: Mistake: Subtracting the atomic number from the wrong value. Fix: Use N = A − Z, where A is the superscript mass number and Z is the subscript atomic number.
Mistake: Saying isotopes have different numbers of protons. Fix: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
Mistake: Saying the second shell has less energy because it is farther away. Fix: A shell farther from the nucleus has greater energy.
Mistake: Treating an electron’s exact path and location as predictable in the modern model. Fix: Explain that its location is described by probability, not a precisely mapped path.
Mistake: Leaving out either protons or neutrons when explaining the nucleus’s mass. Fix: Name both as the heavy particles concentrated in the nucleus.

Mistake: Giving a relative atomic mass calculation without weighting by abundance or dividing by 100. Fix: Multiply each isotope mass by its percentage abundance, add the products, then divide by 100.

shortTheory.question: Why is it said that almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus?
shortTheory.answer: It was also discovered that almost all the mass of an atom is concentrated in the nucleus because both the heavy particles i.e. protons and neutrons are found to be present here.

shortTheory.question: Why are elements different from one another?
shortTheory.answer: The difference in the properties of elements is due to the difference in the properties of their constituent atoms.

shortTheory.question: How many neutrons are present in ²¹⁰₈₃Bi?
Why does the energy of an electron increase as we move from the first shell to the second shell?
shortTheory.answer: The second shell will also be at a definite distance from the nucleus which will, of course, be greater than the first shell and electron present in it will also possess greater value of energy.

shortTheory.question: What is the classical concept of an electron? How has this concept changed with time?
shortTheory.answer: According to this model the electron can revolve around the nucleus of the atom in specific paths called orbits or shells. According to modern approach, electrons are like charged clouds whose location around the nucleus cannot be predicted with one hundred percent certainty.

shortTheory.question: What holds the protons and neutrons together in the nucleus?
shortTheory.answer: In the nucleus these two particles are held together by a strong nuclear force.
